strengths: Introduces a simple, well-motivated dual-scale parameterization (row and column scales) for weight quantization, with a clear conceptual explanation (Fig. 1) of why it helps trade off outlier-induced error between rows and columns.

Proposes a practical, computationally cheap Sinkhorn-Knopp-style algorithm to find the dual scales by minimizing a newly defined 'matrix imbalance' proxy metric, avoiding non-differentiable min/max optimization issues; the comparison against directly optimizing kurtosis (Fig. 2) provides useful evidence that imbalance is a better proxy in this setting.

Very extensive empirical evaluation: multiple model families (Qwen3 0.6B–235B, DeepSeek-V2/V2.5/V3, Llama2/3) at multiple scales (up to 685B parameters), 3-bit and 4-bit precision, uniform and non-uniform (NF4) quantization levels, calibration-free and calibrated (A-SINQ+AWQ) variants, and MoE architectures — this breadth supports claims of generality and architecture-agnosticism.

Reports diverse and less easily gamed metrics beyond perplexity, including flip rates (following Dutta et al.) and preliminary reasoning-trace accuracy/length results, and provides quantization-time benchmarking showing the method is nearly as fast as RTN (1.1x) while being much faster than GPTQ/AWQ.
Includes reasonably thorough ablations (tiling dimension, shift usage, auxiliary precision) and fair accounting of memory overhead via Pareto-front plots rather than only perplexity numbers.
Method is described with enough algorithmic detail (Algorithm 1) and implementation considerations (Eq. 6) to be reasonably reproducible, and the authors state code will be released.
weaknesses: The reported perplexity/flip-rate improvements over strong calibration-free baselines (HQQ, Hadamard+RTN) are often quite small in absolute terms (e.g., many 4-bit Wiki2 differences are within a few hundredths to a few tenths of a point), and no variance/repeated-run statistics or significance testing are given for the main perplexity/flip tables, making it hard to assess how robust the improvements are versus run-to-run noise.

The theoretical link between minimizing 'matrix imbalance' and minimizing actual quantization error (e.g., MSE or end-to-end loss) is argued mostly empirically/heuristically (Fig. 2) rather than derived rigorously; there is no formal proof or bound connecting the proxy metric to the quantities of ultimate interest.

The core idea of using two scale vectors (row and column) for weight matrices is conceptually related to prior per-channel/per-token scaling approaches (e.g., in weight+activation quantization literature); the paper could more clearly delineate what is fundamentally new beyond combining an existing idea with a Sinkhorn-style normalization procedure, since the primary novel technical contribution appears to be the alternating normalization algorithm rather than dual-scaling itself.

Reasoning-benchmark results (Sec. A.1) are explicitly labeled preliminary and limited to a single model/bit-width and two AIME sets, which is a fairly thin basis for claims about preserved reasoning capability.

The additional forward-pass complexity/overhead from the second (column) scale, and its interaction with activation-quantized (W+A) inference pipelines, is only briefly discussed (Eq. 6) and not empirically benchmarked for actual inference latency/throughput, despite motivation citing compute-bound scenarios in the introduction.

The paper's own ablations (Fig. 4) show that tiling choice and precision of auxiliaries have only minor effects, and some baseline numbers (e.g., HQQ on Llama models in Table 8) appear to underperform substantially relative to other baselines in ways not fully discussed, raising questions about baseline tuning fairness.

strengths: The core idea (row+column 'dual scale' normalization via a Sinkhorn-Knopp-style procedure) is simple, cheap to compute, and architecture-agnostic, requiring no calibration data and no cross-layer interaction, which is a practical advantage over Hadamard/rotation-based methods.

Very broad empirical coverage: Qwen3 (0.6B-235B), DeepSeek-V2/V2.5/V3, Llama 2/3, several MoE architectures, 3-bit/4-bit settings, uniform and non-uniform (NF4) quantization levels, and combination with calibration (AWQ/A-SINQ), giving a reasonably comprehensive picture of where the method helps.

Consistent (if often small) improvements over RTN/HQQ/BnB baselines in perplexity and especially in the flip-rate metric, which the authors argue is a more robust indicator of quantized-model fidelity than raw accuracy.
Quantization is fast (close to RTN cost, much cheaper than GPTQ/AWQ), which matters for the stated calibration-free use case.

Reasonable ablations on tiling (1D/2D), shift usage, and auxiliary precision, and a sensible illustration (Fig. 2) that the proposed imbalance proxy correlates with easier quantization better than kurtosis in this setting.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited and under-contextualized: alternating row/column standard-deviation normalization is essentially classical matrix balancing/equalization (closely related to Sinkhorn scaling, Smoothquant-style channel equalization, and other symmetric scaling preconditioners used in numerical linear algebra). The paper does not clearly differentiate its contribution from this broader literature or discuss why a 'new' proxy metric was needed rather than adapting known balancing criteria.

The central motivating claim of the paper -- that a carefully designed uncalibrated uniform quantizer can match calibrated/non-uniform methods -- is only partially supported: Table 5 shows A-SINQ (calibrated) and calibration-free SINQ beat calibrated baselines only in a minority of highlighted cases, while in most settings calibration still yields a clear improvement over calibration-free SINQ. This overstates the generality of the headline claim.

No theoretical analysis connects the proposed 'matrix imbalance' metric to an actual quantization error bound; the justification in Sec. 2.2.1 and Fig. 2 is empirical and limited to a single small model (Qwen3-1.7B) with a handful of layers, which is a thin basis for a claimed general 'proxy target for quantization.'

No convergence guarantees or complexity analysis are given for the modified Sinkhorn-Knopp procedure, despite claims of being a 'fast algorithm'; practical heuristics (log-domain accumulation, clipping, early stopping) are mentioned but not ablated or justified quantitatively.

Important and directly relevant rotation-based baselines explicitly discussed in Related Work (QuaRot, SpinQuant, FlatQuant, DuQuant, Kurtail) are never empirically compared against, even though the paper repeatedly contrasts itself with 'rotated' approaches; only a weak Hadamard+RTN proxy is used, likely underselling the competitiveness gap.

Many reported perplexity gains are very small (hundredths to tenths of a perplexity point, e.g., Table 1, Table 4) with no variance/confidence intervals or multiple seeds reported for the main accuracy/perplexity tables (only quantization-time has error bars), making it hard to assess statistical significance of the claimed improvements.

The tiling/parameter-matching argument (square tiles needed to match standard single-scale parameter counts) is only valid for square matrices, yet LLM weight matrices are generally non-square; the practical overhead and fairness of memory comparisons in the non-square, 1D-tiling case used throughout the main experiments is not clearly justified.

The reasoning-benchmark evaluation (Table 6) is explicitly called 'preliminary,' uses very small test sets (AIME 2024/2025, each with only 30 problems) and a single model/bit-width, which is too limited to support claims about preserved reasoning capability.
The code/data availability link is left blank ('available at .'), so reproducibility cannot be verified at review time despite claims of easy reproducibility.

Presentation issues: Figure 2's six small subplots are hard to parse, and some notation (e.g., Eq. 4's pseudo-pytorch max/min formulation) is informally specified without a precise mathematical definition, reducing clarity for readers trying to reimplement the method exactly.

strengths: Simple, well-motivated idea: adding a second scaling axis (dual-scaling) to quantization tiles, which provides a principled way to trade off outlier-induced errors between rows and columns rather than being forced to absorb them along a single axis.

Introduces a new proxy metric (matrix imbalance) together with an efficient Sinkhorn-Knopp-style normalization algorithm; the paper empirically justifies this proxy against the previously proposed kurtosis proxy (Fig. 2), showing that minimizing imbalance better tracks end-to-end perplexity than directly minimizing kurtosis.

Extremely broad and convincing empirical evaluation: multiple model families (Qwen3 0.6B-235B, DeepSeek-V2/V2.5/V3, Llama 2/3) at multiple bit-widths (3-bit, 4-bit), including dense, MoE, and MLA architectures, which supports the claim of architecture-agnosticism.

Demonstrates composability with existing techniques: works with calibration (A-SINQ + AWQ), non-uniform quantization levels (NF4), and both 1D/2D tiling, consistently improving over respective baselines.

Reports multiple complementary metrics (perplexity, flip rate, accuracy, reasoning benchmarks with trace length) rather than relying on a single potentially misleading metric, following best practice from Dutta et al.
Quantization is fast (close to RTN speed, much faster than HQQ/GPTQ/AWQ), which is practically important and clearly quantified with timing experiments.
Fair effort to control for parameter/memory overhead via Pareto plots across memory vs. perplexity, rather than only matching bit-width nominally.
Code availability is mentioned, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: The connection between the proposed imbalance proxy and actual quantization error/end-to-end quality is argued largely empirically (via one model, Qwen3-1.7B, in Fig. 2) rather than through theoretical analysis bounding quantization error as a function of imbalance; broader validation of this specific finding across more models would strengthen the core methodological claim.

Many of the gains over the strongest calibrated baselines (e.g., AWQ, GPTQ) are quite small in several settings (Tables 2, 5, 10), and no variance/seed information is given for perplexity or flip-rate results, making it hard to assess the statistical significance of reported improvements.

The paper focuses only on 3-bit and 4-bit regimes; no results are shown for more aggressive 2-bit quantization, where dual-scaling/outlier trade-offs might matter most and where competing rotation-based methods are often evaluated.

While memory overhead is reported, there is no evaluation of actual inference latency/throughput with the extra elementwise scaling step (Eq. 6), leaving the practical runtime cost of the dual-scale parameterization during serving unverified.

The explanation of tiling trade-offs (1D vs 2D, parameter count matching) is somewhat informal; a more rigorous accounting of auxiliary parameter overhead versus the baselines compared against would improve clarity.

Limitations and potential failure modes (e.g., scenarios where imbalance minimization might not help, interaction with extreme outliers, numerical stability details of the log-domain clipping/early stopping) are only briefly mentioned rather than systematically discussed.

strengths: Novel and conceptually simple idea: adding a second-axis (dual) scale factor combined with a Sinkhorn-Knopp-style balancing algorithm that trades off row vs. column quantization error, addressing a clear limitation of single-scale calibration-free quantizers.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation across many model families and scales (Qwen3 0.6B-235B, Llama2/3, Phi-2/3/4, DeepSeek-V2/V2.5/V3), including dense and MoE/MLA architectures, demonstrating broad applicability with essentially no architecture-specific tuning.

Consistent and often substantial perplexity/flip-rate improvements over strong calibration-free baselines (RTN, HQQ, Hadamard+RTN, BnB) at both 3-bit and 4-bit precision, closing a large fraction of the gap to BF16.

Interesting empirical/theoretical analysis linking column-wise weight standard deviation to average input activation magnitude (via a simplified single-layer Adam training argument), offering a plausible mechanistic explanation for why SINQ approximates activation-awareness without calibration data.

Practical, systems-level considerations are addressed: measured memory overhead, inference-time overhead (~1-2% with kernel-level test, near-zero with no-overhead variant absorbing scales into adjacent layers), and quantization time (only ~1.1x RTN, much faster than GPTQ/AWQ).

Demonstrated compatibility/synergy with orthogonal techniques: non-uniform levels (NF4), calibration (ASINQ combined with AWQ/GPTQ), and GGUF/llama.cpp, plus end-to-end throughput results in SGLang, indicating real deployment value.

Reasonably thorough ablations (shift usage, auxiliary precision) and additional evidence such as kurtosis reduction and activation- vs. weight-reconstruction error comparisons against Hadamard rotation, supporting the mechanistic story.
Code and evaluation settings are provided/cited for reproducibility, and open-weight permissively licensed models are used throughout.
weaknesses: The core theoretical justification (Eq. 4, single linear layer + Gaussian input + Adam) is a substantial simplification of real transformer training dynamics; the leap from this toy analysis to explaining the empirically observed correlation in large pretrained LLMs (Fig. 2a) is asserted rather than rigorously established, and the R^2 histograms in Fig. 2a/6 show considerable variance across layers, undermining the claimed general predictive strength.

Several baseline numbers are self-implemented (marked with daggers) rather than taken from original papers or standardized benchmarking suites, which introduces potential for implementation bias favoring the proposed method, especially since some self-run baselines (e.g., Hadamard+RTN) appear weaker than expected in places.

Against non-uniform code-book-based methods (QuIP#, QTIP) in Table 17, ASINQ is roughly on par or slightly worse rather than better, which somewhat weakens the paper's broader competitiveness claims relative to more sophisticated (if less practical) alternatives; this limitation is understated in the main narrative.

The benefit of combining SINQ with non-uniform quantization (NF4) over uniform SINQ is often marginal (Table 3), and in the 32B case uniform slightly outperforms NF4, suggesting the paper's claim of strong synergy with non-uniform levels is somewhat overstated.

No variance/uncertainty reporting (e.g., across random seeds or calibration subsets) for the main perplexity results, making it harder to assess whether some of the smaller reported gains (e.g., a few hundredths of a perplexity point in several 4-bit rows) are meaningful versus noise.

Much of the paper's evidentiary weight is pushed into a very large appendix (19 tables, multiple figures), leaving the main text feeling like a subset of a larger, less tightly curated study; this makes it harder for readers to evaluate the core claims without extensive appendix cross-referencing.

Limited discussion of failure modes or settings where the proposed pseudo-activation-awareness assumption might break down (e.g., architectures/training regimes where weight statistics are not predictive of activation magnitudes), despite the method being proposed as broadly architecture-agnostic.

strengths: The paper identifies an interesting empirical phenomenon: column-wise weight standard deviations in LLM weight matrices correlate with the magnitude of the activations that layer received during training, enabling calibration-free 'pseudo-activation-aware' quantization. The finding is cross-validated across multiple model families (Qwen3, Llama2, Phi-2) in the appendix.

The proposed dual-scale (row and column) parametrization with a Sinkhorn-Knopp-style balancing algorithm is a simple, architecture-agnostic modification that can be layered on top of existing quantizers (RTN, AWQ, NF4), and the paper demonstrates this compatibility empirically.

Extremely extensive experimental validation: multiple model families and scales (0.6B to 685B, including MoE and MLA architectures), multiple bit-widths (3/4-bit), uniform and non-uniform quantization, calibrated and uncalibrated settings, perplexity and flip-rate/accuracy metrics, reasoning benchmarks, inference-time and quantization-time overhead measurements, and comparisons against a wide set of strong baselines (HQQ, GPTQ, AWQ, Hadamard/QuaRot-style rotation, HIGGS, CrossQuant, QuIP#, QTIP, BnB).

Practical considerations are well addressed: the paper reports actual memory overhead of the extra scale vector, provides a 'no-overhead' variant that absorbs scales into neighboring layers, and reports end-to-end throughput on real kernels (gemlite, SGLang, llama.cpp/GGUF), which supports deployability claims.

Code and implementation details are provided, supporting reproducibility, and the method's low quantization-time overhead (close to RTN) is a meaningful practical advantage over calibrated baselines like AWQ/GPTQ.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for the central claim (Eq. 4, weight std. ∝ 1/sqrt(input scale)) rests on a highly simplified single linear layer trained with Adam on a noisy Gaussian target; it is not clearly established that this toy analysis explains the behavior of deep, multi-layer transformers trained with complex objectives, normalization layers, and attention, making the mechanistic claim more suggestive than rigorously demonstrated.

The strength of the correlation between column weight std. and activation magnitude (Fig. 2a, Fig. 6) is reported only via histograms of per-layer R² without summary statistics (mean/median, variance across layers) in the main text, and the correlation visibly varies substantially across layers, so the 'strong predictive power' claim is not quantitatively substantiated as strongly as the narrative suggests.

Reported perplexity improvements, while consistent, are often fairly small in the 4-bit regime (e.g., well under 1 point of perplexity in several Table 1 and Table 4 entries), and the headline '>50% perplexity gap reduction' claim appears driven disproportionately by 3-bit settings and weak RTN/Hadamard baselines rather than uniformly across all configurations, which somewhat overstates the generality of the improvement.

There are internal inconsistencies that undercut the 'SINQ dominates' narrative: e.g., SINQ(NF4) sometimes underperforms SINQ uniform (Table 3, 32B case), AWQ beats A-SINQ on MMLU flips/accuracy for the 32B model in places (Table 2, Table 4), and the code-book comparison (Table 17) shows SINQ roughly matching or trailing QuIP#/QTIP, which is not strongly foregrounded in the main narrative.

Algorithm 1 (the Sinkhorn-style procedure) is presented without convergence analysis or discussion of the sensitivity to hyperparameters (number of iterations K, clamp bounds smin/smax); no ablation over these hyperparameters is provided, which limits understanding of robustness and reproducibility of the core algorithmic contribution.

The 'architecture-agnostic, no cross-layer interaction' claim is weakened by the admission that the no-overhead variant requires sharing the second scale across groups of layers (e.g., Q/K/V, Gate/Up) in many model families, introducing a dependency and an accuracy/overhead trade-off that is only briefly addressed (Appendix A.6) rather than analyzed in depth.

The explanatory mechanism relies on specific training dynamics (Adam-style optimization) and may not generalize to models trained with different optimizers or future training regimes; this limitation is not discussed, raising concerns about the durability of the core assumption as training recipes evolve.

No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported for perplexity/accuracy results, making it hard to assess whether some of the reported small improvements are robust rather than noise.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuinely interesting and useful empirical phenomenon: column-wise weight standard deviations correlate strongly (high R^2) with input activation magnitudes across multiple model families (Qwen3, Llama2, Phi), providing a plausible, partially theoretically motivated (via the Adam update outer-product argument) justification for calibration-free pseudo-activation-aware quantization.

The proposed dual-scale parameterization and Sinkhorn-Knopp-style normalization algorithm is simple, architecture-agnostic (no cross-layer dependencies unlike Hadamard-based methods), and has negligible computational/memory overhead, which is empirically verified (Tables 5, 6, 10).

Extensive experimental validation across many model families and scales (Qwen3 0.6B–235B, Llama2/3, Phi, DeepSeek-V2/V2.5/V3, MoE models), multiple bit-widths (3-bit, 4-bit), and multiple quantization paradigms (uniform/non-uniform, calibrated/uncalibrated), showing consistent improvements over strong baselines (RTN, HQQ, Hadamard+RTN, GPTQ, AWQ, NF4/BnB, HIGGS).

Good ablations (shift vs. no-shift, fp16 vs int8 auxiliaries) and mechanistic analysis (kurtosis increase explanation, matrix vs activation reconstruction error trade-off in Fig. 3) that support the claimed mechanism rather than just reporting end results.
Reasonable reproducibility: code provided, evaluation protocol borrowed from established prior work (Zheng et al. 2025), permissively licensed open-weight models used.

The method is complementary/orthogonal to calibration and non-uniform quantization, and the paper demonstrates this compatibility (ASINQ, SINQ+NF4), increasing its practical usefulness as a drop-in preprocessing step (e.g., GGUF improvement in appendix).
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation of the relationship between column weight std and input scale (Eq. 4) is based on an extremely simplified single-layer, single Adam-step setting with Gaussian inputs/targets; it is not clear how well this toy analysis generalizes to deep multi-layer transformer training dynamics beyond the empirical correlation shown, leaving the causal mechanism somewhat hand-wavy despite being evocative.

The Sinkhorn normalization algorithm (Alg. 1) and the imbalance metric I(W) are introduced somewhat ad hoc without a formal convergence guarantee or theoretical analysis of why minimizing this particular imbalance objective is optimal for quantization error versus other possible normalization objectives.

Improvements over the strongest uncalibrated baseline (HQQ) are often modest in the 4-bit setting (e.g., Qwen3-32B 4-bit: 7.74 vs 8.62 is large, but Qwen3-14B 4-bit: 8.76 vs 8.78 is marginal), and in some cases calibration-free SINQ underperforms calibrated baselines (e.g., Table 4, 4-bit Qwen3-32B: SINQ 20.73 mem/7.74 vs AWQ 7.79 at lower memory 20.00), making the practical significance of the 'uncalibrated closes the gap' claim somewhat overstated in places.

The dual-scale parameterization with shifts introduces extra auxiliary parameters per tile (M additional parameters) and, in the non-'no-overhead' variant, a nontrivial engineering requirement (sharing input scales across Q/K/V and Gate/Up projections) that trades off output quality against inference overhead; the quality degradation from the no-overhead variant (Table 8) is not negligible in some cases (e.g., 1.7B: 17.63 vs 17.14) and this trade-off could be discussed more thoroughly in the main text rather than relegated to the appendix.

No statistical significance testing or variance across random seeds/calibration subsets is reported for the perplexity results, making it hard to assess whether some of the smaller improvements (e.g., hundredths of a point) are meaningful versus noise.

The comparison methodology mixes self-implemented baselines (marked with †) with reported numbers from other papers in several tables, which could introduce inconsistencies in evaluation protocol (e.g., different group sizes, context lengths) though the paper claims to follow Zheng et al. 2025 settings throughout.

The paper's claim of being 'calibration-free' is nuanced since it still requires knowledge of weight matrix statistics at quantization time (though not activation calibration data) -- this terminology distinction could be made clearer earlier, as some readers might initially expect zero data/statistics usage at all.
